title: Protein Intake and Satiety
evidence_summary: Higher protein intake (1.6–2.2 g/kg body weight) is associated with greater satiety, reduced caloric intake, and preservation of lean mass during weight loss.
source_reference: Morton RW et al. (2018). A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults. British Journal of Sports Medicine.

title: Mediterranean Diet and Cardiovascular Health
evidence_summary: The Mediterranean diet pattern (high in vegetables, fruits, legumes, whole grains, olive oil, and fish; low in red meat and processed foods) is strongly associated with reduced cardiovascular risk.
source_reference: Estruch R et al. (2018). Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease with a Mediterranean Diet Supplemented with Extra-Virgin Olive Oil or Nuts. NEJM.

title: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines for Adults
evidence_summary: Adults should do at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity. Additional strength training ≥2 days/week reduces all-cause mortality risk.
source_reference: WHO (2020). WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour.

title: Sleep Duration and Metabolic Health
evidence_summary: Short sleep duration (<7 hours/night) is associated with increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Adults should aim for 7–9 hours per night.
source_reference: Cappuccio FP et al. (2008). Meta-analysis of short sleep duration and obesity in children and adults. Sleep.

title: Daily Water Intake Recommendations
evidence_summary: The European Food Safety Authority recommends 2.0 L/day for women and 2.5 L/day for men from all beverage and food sources. Pre-meal water consumption (500 ml) may reduce caloric intake by ~13%.
source_reference: EFSA (2010). Scientific opinion on dietary reference values for water. EFSA Journal.

title: Fibre Intake and Gut Health
evidence_summary: A diet high in dietary fibre (≥25–30 g/day) from whole grains, vegetables, and legumes improves glycaemic control, reduces LDL cholesterol, and supports a diverse gut microbiome.
source_reference: Reynolds A et al. (2019). Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The Lancet.

title: Exercise and Depression / Anxiety
evidence_summary: Regular aerobic exercise (3–5 sessions/week, 30–45 min) has a moderate-to-large effect on reducing depressive and anxiety symptoms, comparable to pharmacotherapy in mild-to-moderate cases.
source_reference: Cooney GM et al. (2013). Exercise for depression. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.

title: Reducing Ultra-Processed Food Consumption
evidence_summary: Each 10% increment in ultra-processed food intake is associated with a 12% higher all-cause mortality risk. Replacing UPFs with whole foods improves nutrient density and weight outcomes.
source_reference: Rico-Campà A et al. (2019). Association between consumption of ultra-processed foods and all cause mortality. BMJ.

title: Benefits of Walking 8,000–10,000 Steps/Day
evidence_summary: Walking 8,000–10,000 steps/day is associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events compared to <4,000 steps/day, with benefits plateauing around 10,000.
source_reference: Saint-Maurice PF et al. (2020). Association of Daily Step Count and Step Intensity with Mortality Among US Adults. JAMA.

title: Sleep Hygiene and Circadian Alignment
evidence_summary: Consistent sleep and wake times, limiting blue-light exposure 1 hour before bed, and keeping bedroom temperature at 16–18°C improve sleep latency and duration by aligning with circadian rhythm.
source_reference: Irish LA et al. (2015). The role of sleep hygiene in promoting public health: A review of empirical evidence. Sleep Medicine Reviews.
